title: Case Study 11: Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23) (Article 21 — Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal))
legalTheme: Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23) • Article 21 & Right to Shelter
factualMatrix: In a matter instituted before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction), the Petitioner—an aggrieved citizen/association affected by a recent University / Statutory Licensing Board action—challenged the constitutionality and procedural validity of an impugned licensing restriction and regulatory directive touching upon Article 21 (Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23)). The Petitioner contended that Core constitutional framework under Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23). Further, relying on the evolution of doctrine through Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), the Petitioner argued that the State failed to satisfy the strict constitutional threshold and acted with manifest arbitrariness.
framingQuestions: 1. Whether the Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal) before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction) is maintainable in light of Article 21 and constitutional remedies?

2. How does the principle of Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23) (Right to Shelter) apply to the impugned licensing restriction and regulatory directive issued by the University / Statutory Licensing Board?
3. What is the controlling effect of Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973) on the validity of the State/Respondent's action and what relief follows?
statutoryApplicability: Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)
modelAnswer:
1. MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 21): Under the constitutional scheme governing Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23), a Writ Petition (Civil/Criminal) before the Supreme Court of India (Article 32 Writ Jurisdiction) is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 21 or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23)): Core constitutional framework under Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23). Applying the core concept of 'Right to Shelter', the impugned licensing restriction and regulatory directive by the University / Statutory Licensing Board must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Article 21 textually reads: 'No person shall be deprived of his life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.' It applies to all persons (not just citizens) and originally used the phrase 'procedure established by law' borrowed from the Japanese Constitution.

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973)) & RELIEF: Guided by Kesavananda Bharati v. State of Kerala (1973), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 21 is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions. Further, The Drafting Committee, following Sir B.N. Rau's discussions with US Supreme Court Justice Felix Frankfurter, replaced 'due process of law' with 'procedure established by law' to prevent courts from striking down social welfare and land reform legislation on substantive due process grounds.

MAINTAINABILITY & THRESHOLD (Article 23): Under the constitutional scheme governing Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23), a Constitutional Reference before the Constitution Bench (Article 145(3) Reference) is maintainable where a prima facie breach of Article 23 or statutory/constitutional limits is demonstrated. The Court evaluates threshold jurisdiction without permitting procedural technicalities to defeat substantive constitutional justice.

2. DOCTRINAL & STATUTORY ANALYSIS (Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23)): Core constitutional framework under Life, Liberty, Shelter & Untouchability (Articles 21, 21A, 17, 23). Applying the core concept of 'Untouchability', the impugned administrative circular and detention/restraint order by the Municipal Corporation / Panchayat Authority must satisfy legality, rational nexus, and proportionality. As reinforced by Article 17 explicitly states: ''Untouchability' is abolished and its practice in any form is forbidden. The enforcement of any disability arising out of 'Untouchability' shall be an offence punishable in accordance with law.'

3. PRECEDENT APPLICATION (Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978)) & RELIEF: Guided by Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India (1978), any executive or legislative overreach inconsistent with Article 23 is liable to be struck down or suitably moulded by appropriate directions.
